hook.text: In 2015, Volkswagen was caught cheating on emissions tests—on 11 million cars worldwide.

buildup.text: VW's diesel engines had software that detected test conditions and reduced emissions only during tests.

discovery.text: On real roads, those cars emitted up to 40 times the legal limit of nitrogen oxides.

twist.text: VW had marketed these cars as 'clean diesel.' The fraud ran for at least six years.

climax.text: The scandal cost VW over $30 billion in fines and killed the clean diesel movement overnight.

punchline.text: Dieselgate accelerated the shift to electric.

quiz.question: How many VW cars were affected by Dieselgate?

details.summary: In 2015, Volkswagen was caught using software to cheat diesel emissions tests, making cars appear clean in labs while polluting up to 40 times the legal limit on real roads.
details.whyItMatters: Dieselgate shattered public trust in diesel technology, accelerated the shift toward electrification, and resulted in over 30 billion dollars in fines and settlements for Volkswagen.
takeaways: Defeat devices activated clean mode only during lab tests
About 11 million vehicles worldwide were affected
The scandal pushed Volkswagen to invest heavily in EVs

faq.question: How was Volkswagen caught cheating?
faq.answer: Researchers at West Virginia University tested VW diesels on the road and found emissions far exceeding lab results. The EPA then investigated, forcing Volkswagen to admit using defeat devices.

faq.question: Did other automakers also cheat on emissions tests?
faq.answer: Investigations revealed that several other manufacturers, including Fiat Chrysler and Mitsubishi, had used various methods to misrepresent emissions or fuel economy during testing.
